newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices hit 20-year high, gold steady.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices hit 20-year high, gold steady.

text.p: Coffee prices soared to 20-year highs on Thursday in a dizzy rally on frantic buying from speculators and commercial coffee firms worried about small coffee stockpiles and shrinking crop prospects.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery closed at 277.05 cents a pound, up 15.55 cents, after trading as high as 279.00 cents -- the highest price for a coffee futures contract on the exchange since June 1977.
Coffee hit a record high of 340.70 cents in April 1977.
With coffee stockpiles in both consuming and producing countries near 20-year lows, traders have begun to focus on any sign of cool weather in top grower Brazil.

"It is going to turn much colder in Argentina next week," said Weather Services Corp. meterologist Mike Palmerino. "Some of the cool air could spill into Brazil, but it's a far cry from having a freeze in Brazil's coffee areas."
Two severe frosts in 1994, one in late June and another in early July, cut Brazil's 1995/96 crop by some 50 percent and sent futures prices to near 10-year highs.

"The market is still responding to tightness," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "Even though the colder weather next week is not expected to impact the coffee belt, we are getting near to the freeze season and people do not want to be short."
Worries about tight on-hand coffee stocks could ease on a report issued after the market closed on Thursday.

In the monthly report, the Green Coffee Association of New York said stocks of green coffee stored in U.S. warehouses rose in April by 198,000 bags to 1,855,000 bags, a greater increase than many traders expected.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.

But analysts said smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries -- notably second-largest producer Colombia -- and the prospects for a smaller crop next season in top producer Brazil even without a frost remain a concern.
Elsewhere, gold prices edged higher as traders puzzled over German announcements about the fate of gold now held in the vaults of the Bundesbank, the German central bank.
Gold for June delivery at the COMEX in New York closed 20 cents an ounce higher at $348.40 after falling more than $2 on Wednesday when it appeared Germany might sell gold.
But German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Thursday that not a single ounce of Bundesbank gold reserves would be sold.

"The market reacted yesterday when it came out that they might sell some gold, a change of heart for the Germans. But Waigel made it clear they are not going to be selling any gold, just reevaluating it," said Scott Mehlman, chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais Rouse.
Traders said Waigel is trying to fill gaps in his 1997 budget which threaten to keep the country from qualifying for Europe's single currency.
Reevaluating Bundesbank gold to market value could create 40 billion marks in paper profits for Bonn, they said.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices fell after a weekly report showing lower-than-expected exports. Soybeans for May delivery closed down 7 cents a bushel at $8.62.

"We had a low export sales number but it had been expected," said analyst Dale Durchholz at Agrivisor Services, a unit of the Illinois Farm Bureau. "Everybody is pretty dialed into the fact that exports are going to fall because the South Americans are shipping it out as fast as they can."
The Agriculture Department said exports of soybeans in the week ended on May 8 were 141,200 metric tons, when some traders had expected sales as high as 200,000 tons.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices closed lower after Tosco Corp said it reopened its Trainer, Pennsylvania, refinery, which will add about 100,000 barrels a day of gasoline to the market.
Gasoline for June delivery closed 0.34 cent a gallon lower at 64.04 cents.
Trade in other pertroleum markets was featureless, with June crude oil closing down 9 cents a barrel at $21.30 and June heating oil ending up 0.06 cent a gallon at 56.48 cents.
